tips.title: Arterioles widen; capillaries do nothing
tips.body: *The capillaries dilate* and *the capillaries move to the surface* are both wrong, and both are common. A capillary wall is one cell thick with no muscle. Say: **the arterioles widen, so more blood flows near the surface**.

tips.title: It is the evaporation that cools
tips.body: Sweat sitting on the skin does nothing. **Evaporation** takes energy from the skin, which is why sweating works poorly in humid air. An answer that says *sweat cools you* has described rather than explained.

tips.title: Denatured, never killed
tips.body: An enzyme is a protein and was never alive. Heat breaks the bonds holding its shape, so the **active site changes shape** and the substrate no longer fits. That wording is what the mark is for.

tips.title: Shivering is the odd one out
tips.body: Every other response changes the **rate** at which heat is lost. Shivering is the only one that **generates** heat, through increased respiration in the muscles. If a question asks which response produces heat, that is the answer.

tips.title: Cold is reversible, hot is not
tips.body: Too cold merely **slows** enzymes, and warming fixes it. Too hot **denatures** them permanently. That asymmetry is the answer to *why is a high temperature more dangerous*, and it is worth one clean sentence.

why.matters:
A body is held at about **37 °C** for one reason: **enzymes**. Every reaction in every cell is run by one, and an enzyme works only inside a narrow range of temperature.

What makes it urgent is that the two directions are not equally forgiving. Too cold and reactions merely slow, which warming undoes. Too hot and the enzymes **denature**, which nothing undoes. So the control system is not there to keep you comfortable — it is there because one side of the range is permanent.

examples.title: Why you go red in the heat and pale in the cold
examples.body:
The colour is blood. When the hypothalamus detects that you are too hot, the **arterioles** supplying the skin **widen**, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost. Too cold and they narrow, keeping the blood — and the heat — deeper in.

Say arterioles, not capillaries. A capillary has no muscle in its wall and can do nothing of the kind, and capillaries certainly do not *move to the surface*. The vessels that change are the small arteries that feed them.

visual.alt: A table of the responses to being too hot and too cold: arterioles widening or narrowing, sweat produced or not, hairs lying flat or standing up, and shivering, which has no counterpart on the hot side

examples.title: Why sweating fails in a humid room
examples.body:
Sweat sitting on skin cools nothing. It is the **evaporation** that takes energy from the skin, and evaporation needs somewhere for the water vapour to go.

In humid air there is already so much water vapour that very little more can leave, so the sweat stays where it is and you keep the heat — which is why a hot dry day is bearable and a hot damp one is not, and why a fan helps by sweeping the humid layer away rather than by cooling the air.

visual.alt: A flow chart of sweating: when too hot, sweat is produced, and only if it can evaporate does it take energy from the skin and cool the body; in humid air it cannot

examples.title: Why too hot does lasting damage and too cold usually does not
examples.body:
Both are the same control loop overwhelmed, and they harm the body in different ways, for a reason that is pure chemistry.

Cold **slows** enzymes: fewer collisions, less kinetic energy, and everything runs sluggishly — but the enzymes are undamaged, and warming the person up restores them. Heat **denatures** them: the active site loses its shape, and that does not come back on cooling. Severe cold is still dangerous, because reactions can slow too far to keep the body alive, but short of that, warming undoes the effect.

visual.alt: A table contrasting too cold, where enzymes merely slow down and warming restores them, with too hot, where they denature, the active site loses its shape and the change cannot be reversed

steps.title: Why temperature must be controlled
steps.body:
This whole topic is **Biology only** (7.10B to 7.12B). Vasoconstriction and vasodilation (7.12B b and c) are **Higher tier** only.

Human body temperature is held at about **37 °C**, and the reason is **enzymes**.

Every reaction in a cell is controlled by an enzyme, and an enzyme works by its **active site** fitting the substrate. Temperature affects that fit in two opposite ways:

- **Too cold.** The molecules move more slowly, so there are fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate. Reactions become **too slow** to keep the body working. This is **reversible** — warm it up again and the enzyme works as before.
- **Too hot.** The enzyme **denatures**: the bonds holding its shape break, the **active site changes shape**, and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme stops working, and this is **not reversible**.

That asymmetry matters. Being cold slows you down; being too hot damages you permanently. It is why a high fever is dangerous in a way that being chilly is not, and it is why the word **denatured** — not *killed* — is the one to use.

Controlling temperature is therefore part of **homeostasis**: keeping conditions inside the body constant so that cells can work, whatever is happening outside.

steps.title: The skin, and who is in charge
steps.body:
Thermoregulation involves the **skin** as the effector and the **hypothalamus** as the control centre. The specification names three parts, and each has a distinct job.

**The hypothalamus** — in the brain. It contains receptors that **monitor the temperature of the blood** flowing through it, and it receives information from temperature receptors in the skin. It then **coordinates the response**, sending impulses to the skin and muscles. It is the **thermoregulatory centre**.

**The epidermis** — the **outer** layer of the skin. It is a **protective** layer: it forms a barrier against water loss and against pathogens entering. It contains no blood vessels. Its part in temperature control: **sweat reaches the surface through pores in the epidermis**, and evaporates from there, and the hairs grow out through it.

**The dermis** — the **thicker inner** layer, and where almost everything happens. It contains:

- **sweat glands**, which produce sweat
- **blood vessels**, which widen or narrow
- **hair erector muscles**, which raise or lower the hairs
- **receptors**, which detect the temperature of the surroundings
- a layer of **fat** below it, which insulates

So if a question asks which layer holds the sweat glands, blood vessels and hair muscles, the answer is the **dermis**. The epidermis protects, and lets the sweat out through its pores; the dermis responds.

steps.title: Vasodilation, said precisely
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)* This is where answers most often go wrong, so it is worth being exact.

**The blood vessels that change are the arterioles** — the small arteries that supply the skin capillaries. They have muscle in their walls, so they can widen and narrow.

**The capillaries themselves do not change.** They have walls one cell thick with no muscle, so they cannot dilate or constrict. And they certainly do not **move** — a capillary is fixed in the tissue.

So three common phrasings are wrong:

- *The capillaries dilate* — they cannot.
- *The capillaries move closer to the surface* — they do not move at all.
- *The blood vessels move up and down* — nothing moves.

The correct version is one sentence: **the arterioles widen, so more blood flows through the capillaries near the surface, and more heat is lost.**

**What is actually being changed** is the **amount of blood** flowing through the vessels near the surface, not their position. Widening the supply increases the flow; narrowing it reduces the flow.

One more piece of precision: vasodilation does not cool the air or the skin directly. It brings **more warm blood near the surface**, so **more heat is lost from the blood to the surroundings** — which is why it works less well on a very hot day, when the surroundings are nearly as warm as you are.

steps.title: Going deeper: the same loop, a third time
steps.body:
**The pattern you have now seen three times.** Thyroxine, blood glucose and temperature are all controlled the same way:

1. A **receptor** detects a change — here, receptors in the **hypothalamus** monitoring blood temperature, and receptors in the **dermis** detecting the surroundings.
2. A **coordination centre** processes it — the **hypothalamus**.
3. **Effectors** respond — the **blood vessels**, **sweat glands**, **hair erector muscles** and **skeletal muscles**.
4. The response **opposes** the change.
5. As the temperature returns to normal, the response **switches off**.

Writing the answer in that shape earns marks even where you are unsure of a detail, because it shows you understand it as a control system.

**Why there are several responses rather than one.** Each one is limited. Sweating fails in humid air, because sweat cannot evaporate into air that is already saturated — which is why a humid 30 °C feels far worse than a dry 30 °C. Vasodilation fails when the surroundings are as warm as the skin, because heat only flows from hot to cold. Having several mechanisms means the body is not defeated when one of them stops working.

**Shivering is the odd one out, and it is worth noticing why.** Every other response **conserves** heat or **loses** it — it changes the rate at which heat moves. Shivering is the only one that **generates** heat, by increasing respiration. That is also why it is the response of last resort: it costs energy, whereas narrowing a blood vessel is free.

**Three phrasings that cost marks.**

- *The capillaries dilate* or *move to the surface* — no. The **arterioles widen**; the capillaries do nothing.
- *Sweat cools you* — only its **evaporation** does.
- *Enzymes are killed* — they are **denatured**. An enzyme was never alive, and the examiner is testing whether you know what denaturing is.

**And one about hairs.** In humans, hairs standing up traps very little air — it is largely a vestigial response, which is why we get goosebumps rather than genuine insulation. You should still name it, because the specification does, but it explains why shivering matters more to us than it does to a furry animal.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Body temperature is held at about **37 °C** so that **enzymes** work.
- **Too cold**: reactions are **too slow**, and it is **reversible**. **Too hot**: enzymes **denature**, and it is **not**.
- The **hypothalamus** monitors the temperature of the **blood** and coordinates the response.
- The **epidermis** is the outer, **protective** layer; sweat reaches the surface through **pores** in it. The **dermis** holds the sweat glands, blood vessels, hair erector muscles and receptors.
- **Too hot**: **vasodilation** — the **arterioles widen**, so more blood flows near the surface and **more heat is lost**.
- **Sweating**: sweat **evaporates**, and evaporation **takes energy from the skin**.
- **Hairs lie flat**, trapping less air.
- **Too cold**: **vasoconstriction** — the **arterioles narrow**, so **less heat is lost**.
- **Shivering**: muscles contract rapidly, increasing **respiration**, which **releases energy as heat**. It is the only response that **generates** heat.
- **Hairs stand up**, trapping air as insulation, and **sweating stops**.
- The **capillaries do not dilate or move** — only the **arterioles** change.
- Say **denatured**, not killed; and say the **evaporation** cools, not the sweat.
- Several mechanisms exist because each one fails under some conditions.

questions.prompt: Explain how the body responds when its temperature rises above normal, naming the part of the brain involved and describing three responses.
questions.solution: The hypothalamus, which is part of the brain, contains receptors that monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through it, and it also receives information from temperature receptors in the dermis of the skin. When it detects that the body temperature has risen above normal it coordinates a response. First, vasodilation occurs: the arterioles that supply the capillaries near the surface of the skin widen, so that more blood flows through those capillaries and more heat is lost from the skin to the surroundings. It is important to note that the capillaries themselves do not widen or move, because their walls are only one cell thick and contain no muscle. Second, the sweat glands in the dermis release sweat on to the surface of the skin. The sweat then evaporates, and evaporation takes energy from the skin, which cools it. Third, the hair erector muscles relax so that the hairs lie flat, trapping less air and therefore providing less insulation. Together these responses reduce the body temperature back towards thirty seven degrees Celsius, and as it returns to normal the responses are switched off, which makes this an example of negative feedback.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Detection.** The **hypothalamus** contains receptors monitoring the temperature of the **blood**, and receives information from receptors in the **dermis**. It coordinates the response.

**Response 1 — vasodilation.** The **arterioles** supplying the skin capillaries **widen**, so **more blood flows** through the capillaries near the surface and **more heat is lost** to the surroundings.

Say *arterioles*. The capillaries do not widen — their walls are one cell thick with no muscle — and they do not move.

**Response 2 — sweating.** The **sweat glands** in the **dermis** release sweat on to the skin. The sweat **evaporates**, and **evaporation takes energy from the skin**, cooling it.

The cooling is the evaporation, not the sweat.

**Response 3 — hairs lie flat.** The erector muscles **relax**, so **less air is trapped** and there is less insulation.

**The result.** Temperature falls back towards **37 °C**, and as it does the responses switch off — negative feedback, the same shape as thyroxine and blood glucose.

questions.prompt: Explain why the human body must keep its internal temperature close to 37 °C, referring to enzymes, and explain why a high temperature is more dangerous than a low one.
questions.solution: Every chemical reaction that takes place in a cell is controlled by an enzyme, and an enzyme works because its active site has a shape that fits the substrate. If the body temperature falls too low, the molecules move more slowly and there are fewer collisions between the enzyme and the substrate, so the reactions in cells become too slow to keep the body functioning properly. This effect is reversible, because warming the body up again restores the normal rate of reaction. If the body temperature rises too high, the bonds that hold the enzyme in its shape break and the enzyme becomes denatured, which means that its active site changes shape so that the substrate no longer fits into it. The enzyme then stops working altogether, and this change cannot be reversed by cooling the body down again. A high temperature is therefore more dangerous than a low one, because the damage it does to enzymes is permanent while the effect of being too cold is not.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why enzymes matter.** Every reaction in a cell is controlled by an **enzyme**, and an enzyme works because its **active site** fits the substrate.

**Too cold.** Molecules move more **slowly**, so there are **fewer collisions** between enzyme and substrate. Reactions become **too slow** to keep the body working.

This is **reversible**: warming the body restores the normal rate.

**Too hot.** The bonds holding the enzyme's shape **break**, so the enzyme is **denatured** — the **active site changes shape** and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme stops working.

This is **not reversible**: cooling down does not restore the shape.

questions.prompt: On a day when the air temperature is 40 °C, a person's skin arterioles are fully widened, yet their body is still gaining heat. Which statement best explains why vasodilation is not cooling them?
questions.solution: **Heat only flows from hotter to cooler.** Vasodilation widens the arterioles so that more warm blood flows through the capillaries near the surface, and heat is lost from that blood **to the surroundings**. That works only while the surroundings are cooler than the blood. When the air is at 40 °C and the blood at 37 °C, the flow of heat reverses: the blood near the surface warms up. On a day like this the body depends on **sweating**, because evaporation removes energy from the skin whatever the air temperature, provided the air is not too humid. Widening the arterioles brings blood towards the surface, not away from it; it is the body's own temperature, not the air's, that decides whether proteins denature; and capillaries have no muscle in their walls, so they cannot dilate.

markScheme.description: heat flows from hotter to cooler, so blood near the surface gains heat from air hotter than itself

options: Widening the arterioles sends blood deeper into the body, so the warm blood never reaches the capillaries near the surface
At 40 °C the muscle in the arteriole walls denatures, so the arterioles stop responding to impulses from the hypothalamus
Heat flows from hotter to cooler, so blood near the surface at 37 °C gains heat from the hotter air instead of losing heat to it
In hot air the capillaries dilate as well, which slows the blood down so much that no heat can be carried out of the body at all

questions.prompt: An athlete finishes a race on a cool day, sweating heavily. A few minutes after stopping, the athlete begins to shiver. Which statement explains why the shivering starts?
questions.solution: **The sweat keeps evaporating.** During the race, the working muscles released a great deal of heat, and the body responded by sweating. When the athlete stops, the muscles stop producing heat but the sweat is still on the skin, and it goes on evaporating, taking energy from the skin and cooling the blood that flows beneath it. Receptors in the **hypothalamus** detect the falling blood temperature and send impulses to the skeletal muscles, which contract rapidly: **shivering**. The contractions increase respiration in the muscles, releasing energy as heat. Shivering is coordinated by the hypothalamus, not by the muscles or the air acting on their own, and lactic acid causes fatigue, not shivering.

markScheme.description: sweat keeps evaporating and cools the blood; the hypothalamus detects the fall and triggers shivering

options: Lactic acid built up in the muscles during the race makes the muscle fibres twitch on their own once the running stops
The cool air acts directly on the muscles of the arms and legs, which contract as a reflex that does not involve the brain at all
The heart rate falls when the race ends, so less warm blood reaches the muscles and they contract to pull blood back into them
Sweat left on the skin keeps evaporating, taking energy from the skin and cooling the blood, which the hypothalamus detects

questions.prompt: Give the name of the change that happens to an enzyme when a high temperature breaks the bonds holding its shape, so that its active site no longer fits the substrate.
questions.solution: **Denaturation**: the enzyme is **denatured**. If the body's temperature rises much above 37 °C, the bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits, so the reaction stops. The change is permanent, which is why the body holds its temperature at about 37 °C and why being too hot is more dangerous than being too cold. Say *denatured*, never *killed*: an enzyme is a protein molecule, not a living thing.

markScheme.description: denaturation (the enzyme is denatured)

questions.prompt: At rest, the blood flow to a person's skin is 250 cm³ per minute. In a hot room, vasodilation increases the flow to 1 000 cm³ per minute. Calculate the percentage increase in blood flow to the skin.
questions.solution: Increase $= 1\,000 - 250 = 750$ cm³ per minute. Percentage increase $= \dfrac{750}{250} \times 100 = 300\%$. The flow is four times what it was, which is a 300% increase, not 400%: the percentage is the **change** divided by the **original** value. The arterioles supplying the skin capillaries have widened, so far more warm blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost from the blood to the surroundings.

markScheme.description: finds the increase, 750, and divides it by the original 250 (× 100)

questions.prompt: When sweat evaporates from the skin, each gram of sweat takes about 2.4 kJ of energy from the skin. During one hour of running, an athlete lost 0.75 kg of sweat, all of which evaporated. Calculate the mean rate at which evaporation removed energy from the athlete's skin, in kJ per minute.
questions.skill: energy removed by evaporation of sweat
questions.solution: Convert the mass to grams: $0.75 \text{ kg} = 750$ g. Energy removed in the hour $= 750 \times 2.4 = 1\,800$ kJ. Per minute: $\dfrac{1\,800}{60} = 30$ kJ/min. It is the **evaporation** that removes the energy, not the sweat sitting on the skin: the liquid takes energy from the skin as it turns to vapour. That is also why sweating cools you less well in humid air, where the sweat cannot evaporate.

markScheme.description: converts 0.75 kg to 750 g and multiplies by 2.4: 1 800 kJ
divides by 60 minutes
30 kJ/min

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides hard for 30 minutes on a day when the air temperature is 5 °C. By the end, the cyclist's face is flushed red and the cyclist is sweating, even though the air is cold. Explain why the body responds in this way.
questions.skill: responding to heat made inside the body
questions.solution: The working muscles **respire** much faster, and respiration releases energy, much of it as **heat**, which warms the blood: an **internal** change. The **hypothalamus** monitors the temperature of the **blood**, not of the air, so it detects the rise and responds as it would on a hot day. The arterioles supplying the skin capillaries **widen** (**vasodilation**), so more blood flows near the surface, which makes the skin look flushed and transfers more heat to the surroundings. The sweat glands release **sweat**, and as it evaporates it takes energy from the skin. The cold air does not stop the response, because what is being controlled is the core temperature.

markScheme.description: the muscles respire faster during exercise, releasing heat that warms the blood
the hypothalamus detects the rise in blood temperature (not the air temperature) and coordinates the response
vasodilation sends more blood near the surface (flushed skin) and sweat evaporates, so more heat is lost

criteria.text: Explains that the muscles respire faster during exercise, and respiration releases energy as heat, which warms the blood
Explains that the hypothalamus monitors the temperature of the blood, not of the air, so it detects the rise and coordinates a response

Explains that the arterioles supplying the skin capillaries widen (vasodilation), so more blood flows near the surface, making the skin look red, and that sweat evaporates, taking energy from the skin, so more heat is lost

questions.modelAnswer: During hard exercise the leg muscles respire much faster to release the energy needed for contraction, and much of that energy is released as heat. The heat warms the blood flowing through the muscles, so the body temperature starts to rise from the inside. The hypothalamus monitors the temperature of the blood passing through it, not the temperature of the air, so it detects this rise and sends impulses to the skin. The arterioles supplying the capillaries near the surface widen: this is vasodilation. More blood flows close to the surface, which is why the face looks flushed, and more heat is transferred from the blood to the surroundings. The sweat glands release sweat, and as the sweat evaporates it takes energy from the skin, cooling it. The cold air does not prevent these responses, because the body is controlling its core temperature at about 37 °C, and on this ride the heat being made inside is greater than the heat being lost to the air.

questions.prompt: A stroke damages a patient's hypothalamus. The patient's skin is completely unharmed. Explain why this patient's body temperature may rise dangerously on a hot day.
questions.solution: The hypothalamus contains receptors that **monitor the temperature of the blood** flowing through it, and receives impulses from temperature receptors in the skin. It is the **coordination centre**: when the blood is too warm it sends impulses to the effectors in the skin, so the sweat glands release sweat, which evaporates and takes energy from the skin, and the arterioles widen so more heat is lost from the blood. If it is damaged, the rise is not detected or no impulses are sent, so sweating and vasodilation are not switched on even though the skin itself is healthy. Heat is gained faster than it is lost, the temperature rises, and if it rises far enough the **enzymes denature**, which cannot be reversed.

markScheme.description: the hypothalamus contains receptors that monitor the temperature of the blood and receives impulses from temperature receptors in the skin
it coordinates the response, sending impulses to the effectors in the skin: the sweat glands and the arterioles
without it, sweating and vasodilation are not triggered, so heat is gained faster than it is lost and the temperature rises until enzymes may denature

criteria.text: Says that the hypothalamus contains receptors that monitor the temperature of the blood, and receives impulses from temperature receptors in the skin
Says that the hypothalamus coordinates the response by sending impulses to the effectors in the skin, the sweat glands and the arterioles
Explains that with the hypothalamus damaged, sweating and vasodilation are not triggered, so heat is gained faster than it is lost, the temperature rises, and enzymes may denature

questions.modelAnswer: The hypothalamus is the body's thermoregulatory centre. It contains receptors that monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through it, and it receives nerve impulses from temperature receptors in the dermis of the skin. When the blood is too warm, the hypothalamus coordinates the response by sending impulses to the effectors in the skin: the sweat glands release more sweat, which evaporates and takes energy from the skin, and the arterioles supplying the skin capillaries widen, so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost to the surroundings. If the hypothalamus is damaged, the rise in temperature is not detected, or no impulses are sent, so these responses are not switched on even though the sweat glands and arterioles are themselves healthy. On a hot day the body gains heat from the surroundings and from respiration faster than it loses it, so the temperature rises. If it rises far enough, the enzymes in the cells denature: their active sites change shape so the substrate no longer fits, and the change cannot be reversed, which is why the rise is dangerous.

questions.prompt: A person falls into cold water and is pulled out after a few minutes. Explain how the body detects the fall in its temperature and how it responds to bring the temperature back to normal. In your answer, explain why shivering is different in kind from the other responses.
questions.solution: Receptors in the **hypothalamus** monitor the temperature of the blood, and temperature receptors in the skin send impulses to it; it coordinates the response. The **arterioles** supplying the skin capillaries narrow (**vasoconstriction**), so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost to the surroundings; the capillaries themselves do nothing. The **hair erector muscles** contract so the hairs stand up and trap insulating air, and **sweating stops**. The skeletal muscles contract rapidly, **shivering**, which increases respiration and releases energy as heat. Shivering is the odd one out: every other response **reduces heat loss**, while shivering is the only one that **generates heat**. As the blood warms, the responses switch off: the response opposes the change, which is negative feedback, and it matters because too low a temperature slows every enzyme-controlled reaction.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or two responses to cold, such as shivering or hairs standing up, with little explanation of how each works or of how the change is detected

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes detection by the hypothalamus and two or more responses with how each reduces heat loss or releases heat, but with a gap, such as saying the capillaries narrow, or not saying what makes shivering different

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a full account: the hypothalamus monitors blood temperature and coordinates the response; the arterioles narrow so less blood flows near the surface; hairs stand up and sweating stops; shivering increases respiration in the muscles, releasing heat, and is the only response that generates heat rather than reducing its loss; may add that the responses switch off as the temperature returns to normal

criteria.text: Says that receptors in the hypothalamus monitor the temperature of the blood, and that temperature receptors in the skin send impulses to it
Says that the hypothalamus coordinates the response, sending impulses to effectors in the skin and in the skeletal muscles

Explains vasoconstriction: the arterioles supplying the skin capillaries narrow, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost to the surroundings (the capillaries themselves do not narrow)
Explains that the hair erector muscles contract so the hairs stand up and trap insulating air, and that sweating stops so less energy is lost by evaporation
Explains shivering: the skeletal muscles contract rapidly, which increases respiration in them, releasing energy as heat
Explains that shivering is the only response that generates heat, whereas vasoconstriction, raised hairs and the end of sweating all reduce heat loss

questions.modelAnswer:
**Detecting the change.** Cold water takes heat from the skin, and the blood flowing near the surface cools. Receptors in the **hypothalamus** monitor the temperature of the blood passing through it, and temperature receptors in the **dermis** of the skin send nerve impulses to it as well. The hypothalamus is the coordination centre: it compares the temperature with normal, about 37 °C, and sends impulses to the effectors in the skin and in the skeletal muscles.

**Reducing heat loss.** The **arterioles** supplying the capillaries near the surface of the skin narrow: **vasoconstriction**. Less blood flows through the surface capillaries, so less heat is transferred from the blood to the surroundings, and the warm blood is kept deeper in the body. It is the arterioles that narrow, not the capillaries, which have no muscle in their walls. The **hair erector muscles** contract, so the hairs stand up and trap a layer of insulating air next to the skin. **Sweating stops**, so no more energy is taken from the skin by evaporation.

**Generating heat.** The skeletal muscles contract and relax rapidly: **shivering**. Contracting muscles respire faster, and respiration releases energy, some of it as heat, which warms the blood passing through the muscles.

**Why shivering is different.** Every other response works by changing how fast heat leaves the body: vasoconstriction, raised hairs and the end of sweating all **reduce heat loss**. Shivering is the only response that **produces heat**, and it costs glucose and oxygen to do so, which is why it is the response the body turns to when conserving heat is not enough.

**Returning to normal.** As the blood warms, the hypothalamus detects the change and the impulses stop: the arterioles widen again and the shivering ceases. The response opposes the original change and switches itself off once the temperature is back to normal, which is **negative feedback**. It matters because at too low a temperature every enzyme-controlled reaction in the cells runs too slowly to keep the body working.

examTechnique.body:
Start with the hypothalamus detecting the change, then give the responses, then say the temperature returns to normal.

Name the arterioles when describing vasodilation or vasoconstriction, and say what happens to the blood flow rather than to the position of any vessel.

For sweating, say that the sweat evaporates and that evaporation takes energy from the skin.

For shivering, name respiration as the source of the heat.

Use the word denatured about enzymes, and say that the active site changes shape.

If the question asks for three responses, give three: the blood vessels, the sweat glands and the hairs, and add shivering when the body is cold.
examinerErrors: Saying the capillaries dilate or constrict.
Saying blood vessels move closer to or further from the surface.
Saying sweat cools the body without mentioning evaporation.
Saying enzymes are killed rather than denatured.
Saying shivering moves warm blood around rather than releasing heat by respiration.
Giving the epidermis as the layer containing the sweat glands.
Leaving out the hypothalamus when asked how the response is coordinated.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer recognises this as the third example of the same control loop and writes it in that shape: receptor, coordination centre, effector, opposing response, switch-off. It is exact about the arterioles and never has a capillary moving or dilating. It attributes the cooling to **evaporation** and can then explain why humidity defeats it. It notices that shivering is the only response that generates heat rather than redirecting it, and it uses *denatured* precisely, saying what happens to the active site rather than merely naming the word.
